checker.verdict: The numbers are right: every headline value was reproduced from the raw per-horizon variances in the saved cards with the checker's own code (not gates.py), and the job records, the declaration order and the pilot markers are in order. Several conclusions say more than the numbers do. (1) For foundry worlds the block-level sigma_hat is the closure gap of the linear ridge and nothing else, the quantity round 5 used to choose the shortlist; the card re-measures that choice, it does not single the seven out independently. (2) The clock is not a design dial: at equal horizons in world time the two membrane cards agree; the dial is the horizon. (3) The rank correlation of 0.83 is one of several defensible values (0.14 to 0.94). (4) The negative controls test little: seven of twelve can hardly fail at the block level, and the free bodies are dull only through the box declared for them. Ten claims are reworded (edits); no number of the study was changed.

findings.F1_what_sigma_hat_is: sigma_hat = min(w_theta, 1 - c) is two different quantities under one name. In all 62 foundry-family worlds the ridge term binds, so sigma_hat is the linear predictor's closure gap; round 5's checker (F4) already showed that in five of the seven worlds the true simulator predicts 92% to 99% of the variance at 32 ticks, so a learned predictor may close much of that gap. In gliders and vortices the hidden-part term binds, and it is set by the width of the declared prior (the plug-in loss grows about as the square of the move: 0.055 at 10%, 4.6 at 100% of the gliders prior). The prior's width is a design dial the report does not name.
findings.F2_selection: The shortlist was chosen in round 5 by the same ridge's ceilings and by being a candidate again at ticks 2000 to 2240 (round5/foundry/analyze2.py, shortlist rule); the card's late run covers ticks 2000 to 2400. '0.28 to 0.51 in all 21 runs' and 'late equals early in 6 of 7' are therefore replications on new seeds of what the worlds were selected for. What is new: the values hold across two seeds, a late window and 128 px.
findings.F3_controls: See the controls claim. A control that would test the foundry verdict is missing: a world the linear ridge cannot close but a small learned predictor can. The free bodies come closest and pass the ridge term like a shortlisted world.
findings.F4_horizon_not_clock: See the two clock claims. Every block-level verdict of a designed world depends on the fixed window of 4, 8, 16 card ticks; '2% to 6% of the predictable variance' is the 8-tick value (w_theta at 16 ticks: 9% to 27%; at 32 ticks: 32% to 55%).
findings.F5_H1: See the H1 claim. H1 can be refuted only where sigma_hat is low; a world it recommends that turns out easy does not refute it.
findings.F6_like_with_like: The README sets the vortices aside for 'a clock at level 2' and calls foundry 4186 stationary. The gate behind both words reads the block view; at the population level 4186 has the same early-window clock (0.18 to 0.19 against 0.22 to 0.26).
findings.F7_redundant_or_unstable_entries: Redundant: within the foundry family the hidden-part term never decides (w_theta at 8 ticks is 0.25 or more in all 23 shortlisted and candidate worlds), so sigma_hat duplicates the block ceiling; the actions gate (76 of 77) and the learned gate (0 of 77 in run A); the three body-law ceilings (in 21 of 52 worlds with bodies the ridge is no better than constant velocity, so the 'single-body law' is inertia); the kind-share law. Unstable: every population entry (sigma_hat of 4470: 0.89, 0.21, 0.97 in A, B, late), the declared verdict where it rests on them, the body-law ceiling of 6845 (0.09 to 0.46) and 7567 (0.49 to 0.78), the interaction gate of the frozen controls (it flips between runs in all four), the gliders evidence index. Stable and informative: the block ceiling by horizon, PF, body counts and half-lives, the member share, the per-channel tick share.
findings.F8_objects: The card's object entries do not tell the gliders world from the non-interacting control: quiet-step ceilings 0.96 to 0.98 in both, and the tracker reports 19 fusions and fissions per 100 ticks for bodies that never interact (47 for gliders). The quiet-step rule was written after that control looked interacting on the CPU (HYPOTHESES.md says so).
findings.F9_sample_sizes: Per run 32 test states from 8 members at 4 snapshot ticks; the hidden part's weight from 2 directions x 2 replicas, the directions fixed across runs; rare regimes from 16 members (4470: 3 of 32 early members, 95% interval about 2% to 25%).

consequences_for_the_conclusions: 'The card singles out foundry 4186 and 4470': it confirms that round 5's shortlist keeps its linear closure gap on new seeds. Whether that gap survives a learned predictor is the open question, and the exams proposed as next step 2 (data-only against true law) are the right test of it.
'Why round 5's exams were easy' stands at the horizons round 5 used (1 to 16 ticks) and for the priors it used; it is a statement about prior width and horizon, not about the worlds' dynamics.

'The clock is a design dial' should read 'the horizon in world time is a design dial'. Membrane on the slow clock is a membrane exam at 160 to 640 time units, where round 5 (bias2) found learned nonlinear closure 0.14 (320 time units) to 0.25 (640) above a hand block mean, and its 0.24 is the ridge term alone (0.03, 0.16, 0.54 at 4, 8, 16 ticks): the block-level value most likely to shrink.
The card's own test passed, but it could hardly have failed at the block level; treat the card as untested against a hard negative.

H2, as the card reads it, predicts that experiments pay in none of the designed, shortlisted or candidate worlds. If the Lab is to matter, that needs a different world or item design, not a different pick from this list.
